rendered: The paper gives no sensitivity or detection limit for S. typhimurium, either in human serum or in plain solution. The serum experiments only test whether the sensor array can tell bacteria apart (classification). They do not measure how little bacteria it can detect. In spiked human serum, the paper reports that the clusters of all seven bacteria were well classified with almost no overlapping[1] (Fig. 5[2]), and S. typhimurium is among the bacteria tested. Limits of detection appear only in the separate concentration study, and only for other species: P. aeruginosa had an LOD of OD600 =0.0034 (CD,[3] …) and L. monocytogenes presented an LOD of 0.0123 (CD,[4] …). In that same concentration study, S. typhimurium did worse: only partial discrimination was achieved for S. typhimurium and S. aureus[5]. The main text does not give a sensitivity value for S. typhimurium in serum.
